column22:
Long before anyone wrote a law down, they told a story about what happens to someone who breaks it. Storytelling is how a species that forgets everything manages to remember what matters.

A fact tells you that a fire burns. A story about a child who touched one anyway makes you flinch before your hand ever gets close. That's the whole trick of narrative: it converts information into experience, and experience is what actually changes behavior.

This is why every durable institution — religion, law, brand, nation — eventually reaches for story instead of statute. Numbers persuade the part of us that calculates. Stories persuade the part of us that acts.

We are, right now, drowning in information and starving for meaning, and meaning has always arrived dressed as a story.
column23:
An AI model can finish your sentence because it has seen a billion sentences finished before. It cannot want to finish it. That distinction is the whole argument.

Human creativity is downstream of stakes: a deadline that scares you, a grief you can't otherwise name, a joke that could land badly. The work carries a cost to make, and the cost is legible in the result — a hesitation, a scar, a private joke only three people will get.

A model has no evening it is dreading, no funeral it is writing toward. It can imitate the shape stakes leave behind, endlessly and fluently, but it cannot generate the shape from a life it is not living.

What AI is very good at is recombination at a scale no person could manage. What it cannot do is mean it.

column22:
A spreadsheet of casualty figures and a single named child's story will not move the same reader the same way, even though the spreadsheet is more complete. That gap is not a flaw in human attention — it's the whole mechanism storytelling exploits to make abstraction bearable.

Stories compress: a hundred years of a region's history become a grandmother's kitchen table. That compression is lossy, but it's the only form dense enough for most people to actually carry around and pass on.

Organizations that want to be remembered eventually stop reciting mission statements and start telling founding stories instead, because founding stories survive being repeated badly by someone who half-remembers them, and mission statements don't.
column23:
Ask a model to write a poem about loss and it will reach for the same handful of images loss has always produced in its training data — rain, empty chairs, unanswered calls. Ask a grieving person and you might get something that's never been written before, because their loss genuinely hasn't.

The model's output is a weighted average of everything it has read. A human's output is filtered through a single irreplaceable nervous system that has only ever had one life. Creativity, at its most interesting, is precisely the deviation from the average — and averaging is the one operation a model cannot opt out of.

It can be startling, even move you. It cannot be new the way a first-person account of a specific Tuesday is new.
